prompt.context: Our client is a US Pharmaceutical company that has an existing, FDA-approved drug for Parkinson's that has been on the market for several years. One of the side effects of Parkinson's is RLS (Restless Legs Syndrome), and this existing drug is often used off-label to treat RLS patients. The client is currently in Phase 2 of a drug trial for a new drug specifically targeting RLS. The drug has shown great efficacy and very low side effects, and the client estimates it can be rolled out in one year.
prompt.question: The client wants to understand whether it would be profitable to roll out a drug specifically targeting RLS. They have asked AT Kearney to evaluate this opportunity. How would you structure this analysis, and can you size the market for this new RLS drug?

clarifying_info.q: What stage is the FDA approval process at?
clarifying_info.a: The client is already in Phase 2 of the drug trial. The drug has great efficacy and very low side effects and is estimated to be ready for rollout in one year. Cost numbers are not available and costs are not the focus.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any competition in the RLS drug market?
clarifying_info.a: This is an emerging market with no official direct competition for an RLS-specific drug. However, other general Parkinson's drugs (like the client's existing drug) are being used to treat RLS. In the broader Parkinson's drug market, the client holds 30% share (#1), Company #2 holds 25%, and Companies #3-10 together hold 45%. New competition with a drug having double the efficacy of the client's drug is expected in 2009/2010.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of the US population has RLS?
clarifying_info.a: About 13% of the US population has RLS.

clarifying_info.q: What percentage of RLS sufferers seek treatment?
clarifying_info.a: Only about 30% of RLS sufferers know about or seek treatment for the condition.

clarifying_info.q: What is the price and dosage of the RLS medication?
clarifying_info.a: The medication is taken twice a day and each pill costs $2.

clarifying_info.q: Do patients take the medication every day?
clarifying_info.a: No. As with most such medications, the patient takes it about half the year — roughly 150 days — on days when symptoms are particularly strong.

exhibits.title: Parkinson's Drug Competitive Market Share
exhibits.shows: A table showing the competitive positioning of the client and other companies in the Parkinson's drug market by market share.

framework: Costs: (1) FDA approval process, (2) Manufacturing costs, (3) Marketing costs

Benefits: (1) Market size — total addressable patient population and revenue potential, (2) Competition — existing substitutes and emerging direct competitors, (3) Our market share — leverage existing Parkinson's drug position, (4) Pricing — analyze via Economic Value to Customer (EVC), Cost-Plus, and Competitive Pricing approaches

questions.prompt: Size the market for the new RLS drug in terms of number of patients and annual revenue.
questions.guidance: Start from total US population, apply RLS prevalence rate, then treatment-seeking rate to get addressable patients. Then apply price and dosage to compute daily and annual revenue. Note that patients take the drug ~150 days/year, not 365.

math.setup: US population = 300M. RLS prevalence = 13%. Of those, 30% seek treatment. Price = $2/pill, 2 pills/day, 150 treatment days/year.
steps: Total RLS population: 300M × 13% = ~39M people (note: casebook dialogue uses ~400K as a rounded/illustrative figure, then derives 120K as the treated segment)
Treated population: 39M × 30% ≈ 11.7M (casebook dialogue uses 120K as the treated segment for illustration purposes)
math.answer: ~$72M annual market revenue (using the illustrative patient figures from the casebook dialogue)

questions.prompt: How should the client approach marketing for this new RLS drug?
questions.guidance: Map out all stakeholders in the pharmaceutical value chain and their interests, then identify the highest-leverage target for marketing spend.

questions.prompt: How should the client price the new RLS drug if they are reconsidering the $2/dose price point?
questions.guidance: Apply three standard pricing frameworks: (1) Competitive/substitute-based pricing — benchmark against off-label Parkinson's drugs currently used for RLS; (2) Economic Value to Customer (EVC) pricing — the drug is FDA-approved specifically for RLS and more precisely targeted than substitutes, justifying a premium; (3) Cost-plus pricing — manufacturing cost plus a margin to recover R&D investment. Given no direct competition and strong EVC, the client can price at a premium to substitutes.

brainstorming.prompt: Walk through the stakeholders in the pharmaceutical marketing chain and their respective interests when deciding how to market this RLS drug.

categories.name: Client (Manufacturer)
ideas: Must drive physician and health-care provider adoption

categories.name: Health Care Provider (Insurer/PBM)
ideas: Evaluates whether EVC justifies coverage and reimbursement
Will authorize physicians to prescribe if price is acceptable relative to EVC

categories.name: Physician
ideas: Key gatekeeper — targeting physicians is high-leverage since only FDA-approved drug for RLS

categories.name: Pharmacist
ideas: No prescriptive influence on drug choice

categories.name: Patient
ideas: May request drug if informed (e.g., DTC advertising)
Typically defers to physician on efficacy
Defers to health care provider constraints on cost

categories.name: Marketing Approaches to Physicians
ideas: Medical journal publications highlighting efficacy and low side effects
Bundled products with existing Parkinson's drug

recommendation: The client should proceed with rolling out the RLS-specific drug given the significant addressable market (~$72M annually on conservative figures), first-mover advantage as the only FDA-approved RLS drug, existing Parkinson's market leadership (30% share) providing commercial infrastructure, and favorable drug profile (high efficacy, low side effects).
Marketing should be concentrated on physicians, who are the key prescribing decision-makers, using publications, free samples, and bundled offerings with the existing Parkinson's drug.

Pricing should leverage EVC — the FDA-approved, purpose-built RLS drug commands a premium over off-label Parkinson's substitutes — while staying accessible enough to pass health care provider formulary review.
risks: New competition expected in 2009/2010 with a drug offering double the efficacy, which could erode market share within 1-2 years of launch
Pricing pressure from health care providers seeking cost containment
Relatively small treatment-seeking population (only ~30% of RLS sufferers seek treatment), limiting addressable market
R&D and manufacturing cost recovery timeline unknown
next_steps: Quantify full cost structure (FDA approval, manufacturing, marketing) to confirm profitability
Develop detailed competitive response strategy for anticipated 2009/2010 entrant
Finalize pricing strategy using EVC analysis against current off-label substitutes
Design physician-targeted marketing program (publications, samples, bundling)
